items.title: Kenya contains imported Ebola case as country moves towards disease-free status
items.description: Kenya contains imported Ebola case as country moves towards disease-free status Kenya Association of Travel Agents Kenya's Ebola outbreak: Last patient discharged as countdown begins to be being declared free of the virus BBC Kenya Ebola: Last patient discharged as CS Duale cautions citizens in DR Congo The EastAfrican Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, awaits disease-free status Al Jazeera Kenya steps up border health surveillance amid Ebola-free countdown Capital FM Africa
content: Kenya has contained an imported Ebola outbreak without community transmission, with authorities confirming that all patients have recovered or been discharged and the country now entering a 42-day countdown towards an official declaration that it is free of the disease.

The outbreak originated from a Kenyan national who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and travelled through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on October 3, 2026. The Ministry of Health confirmed the country’s first case of Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease on October 6.
The case triggered an extensive public health response involving isolation, laboratory testing, contact tracing and monitoring to prevent further transmission.

Kenya subsequently recorded eight secondary infections, bringing the total to nine confirmed cases. All eight were linked to the initial imported case, involving four family members and four healthcare workers. Crucially, all secondary cases were identified among people already under quarantine, and health authorities reported no transmission into the wider community.
The outbreak resulted in two deaths, while seven patients recovered.

The Ministry of Health identified and monitored 135 contacts linked to the initial case, including individuals in Kenya and abroad. The final patient was discharged on November 11, while the remaining 11 contacts completed their monitoring period without developing symptoms.

The 42-day countdown began on November 12 and, if no new infections are detected, Kenya is expected to be declared Ebola-free on December 23, 2026. The period represents twice the virus’s maximum 21-day incubation period, in line with World Health Organization protocols.

The successful containment effort highlights Kenya’s public health surveillance and emergency response capabilities, including early case detection, laboratory confirmation, isolation facilities, contact tracing and coordination between national and county health authorities.

The World Health Organization has also reported no evidence of transmission outside the identified cluster and no new confirmed cases in Kenya since October 19. In its latest disease outbreak update, the organisation advised against imposing travel or trade restrictions on countries responding to the regional health event.

For Kenya’s travel and tourism industry, the distinction between an imported case and sustained local transmission is particularly important. The outbreak did not result in widespread community transmission or a nationwide shutdown of economic and social activities.

The government has maintained that Kenya remains open for international travel, tourism, trade and business, with no domestic restrictions on movement or public gatherings. Enhanced health screening and surveillance at points of entry remain in place as precautionary measures.

While the outbreak in the DRC continues to require regional vigilance, Kenya’s experience demonstrates the importance of effective disease surveillance and rapid containment in protecting public health and maintaining international travel connectivity.

Matiang’i calls out President Ruto over repeated project launches, unfinished projects
items.description: Jubilee Party Leader and Presidential aspirant Dr. Fred Matiang’i has criticised President William Ruto over what he described as repeated launches and relaunches of projects across counties,
content: Jubilee Party Leader and Presidential aspirant Dr. Fred Matiang’i has criticised President William Ruto over what he described as repeated launches and relaunches of projects across counties.
In addition, Matiang’i accused the government of filling communities with unfinished projects and foundation stones instead of completed developments.
Speaking during his mega Gusii tour, where he engaged residents of Kisii and Nyamira counties, Dr. Matiang’i questioned the President’s repeated project launches, saying:
“Mheshimiwa Rais amekuwa hapa siku nne anaingia kufungua project ambayo amefungua tena. Kazi ya Rais huyu ni kwamba, amejaza county zetu na foundation stones. Uongo kila wakati.”
Dr. Matiang’i also accused the President of using money to influence residents in Kisii, insisting that the people of Kisii and Nyamira identify with the Opposition.
He further criticised the government’s record, citing rising insecurity and questioning its ability to guarantee the safety of Kenyans. He also raised concerns over alleged misuse of public funds.

Dr. Matiang’i was accompanied by PPK Party Leader and Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, PLP Party Leader Martha Karua, Siaya Governor James Orengo, former Education Cabinet Secretary Ezekiel Machogu, Nyamira Senator Erick Okong’o Omogeni, Kitutu Chache South MP Anthony Kibagendi, Bomachoge Borabu MP Obadiah Barongo, Kitutu Masaba MP Clive Gisairo and Bobasi MP Innocent Obiri, among other leaders.

Court puts State on notice over use of AI in public services
items.description: Activists had challenged the absence of a framework governing AI systems across public offices.
content: Activists John Wangai, Peter Agoro and Antony Manyara challenged the absence of a comprehensive framework governing AI systems used across many public offices.

The High Court has given the government six months to complete the development of a national policy and legal framework governing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the country, declining to compel Parliament to enact legislation within 90 days.

Justice Edward Muriithi said the State has a constitutional obligation to take legislative, policy and other measures to protect Kenyans from violations of their fundamental rights, including access to healthcare, adequate housing, sanitation, food, clean water, social security and education.

However, he said the Executive and Parliament must be allowed to complete the ongoing process of developing an AI policy and legislation within a reasonable period, rather than having the court dictate the content or timetable of new laws.
Members of the National Assembly follow proceedings during a past session.

The court orders followed a petition filed by rights activists John Wangai, Peter Agoro and Antony Manyara challenging the absence of a comprehensive framework governing AI systems used across many public offices.
They cited automated tools affecting health insurance, national examinations, recruitment, traffic enforcement, policing and education funding.

They sought to stop alleged high-risk uses pending development of safeguards, including automated exam marking, AI-assisted public recruitment, smart cameras and biometric trackers for instant traffic fines, and facial-recognition surveillance linked to predictive policing.

The petitioners argued that several government agencies were already using, or preparing to deploy, artificial intelligence systems in public services without a comprehensive legal framework to protect citizens.

They identified the Social Health Authority (SHA), which they alleged was using an algorithm to determine or adjust household health insurance contributions; the Kenya National Examinations Council (Knec), over alleged automated marking, grading and generation of examination results; and the Public Service Commission (PSC), over alleged AI-powered shortlisting, ranking and interviewing of candidates for public jobs.
They also cited the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA), claiming it was using smart cameras and biometric trackers linked to automated traffic fines and licence demerit points.

The petitioners further accused the Inspector-General of Police and the Ministry of Interior of deploying AI-integrated surveillance cameras with real-time facial recognition and predictive policing systems.
They also questioned the alleged use of AI-based poverty-scoring models by the Ministry of Education to determine bursaries, scholarships, school funding and Higher Education Loans Board allocations.

They warned that uncontrolled deployment of such technologies could expose Kenyans to deepfakes, election interference, discrimination through automated decisions, job losses, consumer harm, threats to academic integrity and misuse of intellectual property. Other risks cited include cited discrimination, privacy violations, denial of services, identity theft, consumer harm and misuse of intellectual property.
Other systems identified included poverty-scoring models used to allocate bursaries, school capitation and Higher Education Loans Board funding.
CCTV cameras installed on Moi Avenue. The cameras will capture traffic offenders and ensure security within the city.

The petitioners sought declarations that the government had failed to develop an AI policy and law, and orders compelling the Cabinet Secretary and Principal Secretary to prepare a framework and table legislation within separate 90-day periods.

However, the court found that the petitioners had not proved specific constitutional violations. “In the present petition, the court finds that the petitioners have not proved a violation or threat to any right by the respondents,” it said.
SHA said its means-testing model used public data, including the 2021 Kenya Continuous Household Survey. It cited an appeal process for members and denied tracking or profiling individuals.
SHA added that 202,282 members had appealed their assessments. Successful appeals reduced total assessed contributions from Sh58.5 million to Sh54.6 million, a reduction of about Sh3.95 million.
The Public Service Commission also denied using AI in recruitment, saying shortlisting and selection remained manual.
The court found no evidence that Knec had deployed an AI marking system. It also found no proof that the PSC used AI-based shortlisting, ranking or automated interviews.

The government said it launched the Kenya Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 in March 2025. It cited consultations involving public agencies, private companies, academics and county governments, and said a draft National AI and Other Emerging Technologies Policy was published in July 2026.

The strategy covers digital infrastructure, data governance, research, innovation and commercialization. The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy invited public comments on the draft policy, setting August 4, 2026, as the submission deadline.
The judge said the Constitution sets no fixed deadline for enacting an AI law. Courts, he said, should not take over Parliament’s role or dictate the content of legislation.

“The State shall take legislative, policy and other measures, including the setting of standards, to achieve the progressive realization of the rights guaranteed under Article 43 of the Constitution,” he quoted from Article 21(2).

The court noted that existing laws also address some risks. Section 35 of the Data Protection Act protects people from decisions based solely on automated processing where these have legal effects or significantly affect them, and allows requests for reconsideration in specified circumstances.
The petitioners had not identified a specific system or proved that required safeguards were missing.

“There is no doubt that Artificial Intelligence presents serious constitutional questions of possible rights violation,” said Justice Muriithi, noting that the respondents accepted the need for responsible governance.
He said the Executive and Legislature should be allowed to complete their work within a reasonable period of time.
The court dismissed the rights-violation claims but held the delay question in abeyance for six months, allowing policy and legislative work to be completed.
The case is set to be mentioned on May 15, 2027, for further directions.

items.title: Emirates introduces A350 aircraft and Premium Economy on Nairobi–Dubai route
items.description: Emirates introduces A350 aircraft and Premium Economy on Nairobi–Dubai route Kenya Association of Travel Agents
content: Emirates has introduced its Airbus A350 aircraft on the Nairobi–Dubai route, bringing its Premium Economy cabin to the Kenyan market as the airline expands its premium travel offering on one of its three daily services.

The aircraft entered service on November 12, replacing the Boeing 777 on the morning EK717 flight from Dubai to Nairobi and the return EK718 service. The other two daily rotations between Nairobi and Dubai will continue operating with Boeing 777 aircraft.

The introduction gives passengers travelling from Kenya access to Emirates’ Premium Economy product, which sits between Economy and Business Class and offers an additional cabin choice for travellers seeking greater comfort without paying Business Class fares.
The new offering is particularly relevant to passengers connecting through Dubai to long-haul destinations in Europe and the United States, where Emirates operates an extensive international network.
Speaking about the introduction, Emirates said Kenya had become its second-largest African market by capacity after South Africa, underscoring Nairobi’s importance to its continental operations.
The airline indicated that it would continue assessing opportunities to expand its services in Kenya, with future capacity decisions dependent on passenger demand.

Emirates has positioned Premium Economy as a mid-market product, with fares generally sitting approximately halfway between Economy and Business Class. The airline also indicated that the introduction of the A350 would not, in itself, result in a repricing of fares on the Nairobi route.
The aircraft deployment comes as airlines increasingly differentiate their products across cabin classes to attract passengers with varying travel budgets and preferences.

For travel agents, the introduction creates another option when packaging international travel, particularly for clients travelling to Europe and North America through Dubai. Premium Economy provides an alternative for passengers who want additional comfort on long-haul journeys but may not require the full range of services offered in Business Class.
The introduction further strengthens Emirates’ Nairobi operations and expands the range of international travel products available to passengers departing from Kenya.

content: Sierra Leone Telegraph: 15 November 2026:

Nine creators have been named winners across gaming, video and music at CANEX WKND 2026, following the live pitch finale of the CANEX Create-thon, powered by Gebeya. Held on 6 November at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Cultural and Creative Arts in Lagos, the session brought together finalists, industry judges and creative and technology leaders to explore Africa’s opportunities in the artificial intelligence economy.

Organised through the African Export-Import Bank’s (Afreximbank) Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) programme, in partnership with Gebeya and the Afreximbank Innovation Lab, the competition challenged creators to turn African-inspired ideas into working projects using Gebeya’s Dala Studio.
Participants used AI tools within Dala Studio to produce digital games, videos and music, supported by computing resources and technical guidance.

The session- which also marked the official launch of the Afreximbank Innovation Lab-aimed to demonstrate how access to technology can help African creators turn ideas into AI-powered digital creations, while examining the skills, infrastructure and commercial opportunities needed to build sustainable creative businesses.

Alongside the live pitches, a panel discussion explored the theme, “Claiming Our Stake in the AI Revolution”, bringing forth a much-needed conversation on the opportunities as well challenges of this fast-evolving area, as well as what it means for African creators.

According to Gebeya, around 6,000 creators from 43 countries participated in the competition, submitting 792 games, music tracks and videos built on Dala Studio. The top three creators in each category advanced to the live pitch finale.

Speaking at the opening of the session, Temwa Gondwe, Director, Creatives and Diaspora at Afreximbank, emphasised that Africa’s creative influence must translate into greater ownership and economic returns. He called for affordable computing power, accessible creative tools, effective distribution channels and stronger protection of creators’ intellectual property.
“The question is not whether Africa will participate. The question is how much value Africa will create and own and retain,” Gondwe said.
He highlighted the importance of connecting creators with investors, buyers and audiences, arguing that access to technology must be accompanied by opportunities to build sustainable businesses.

The competition offered a total prize pool of US$50,000. Under its published award structure, first-, second- and third-place prizes in each category are US$7,000, US$3,500 and US$1,500 respectively, with additional awards for qualifying creators from the top 20 African countries.

The live pitch judging panel comprised Oluwasemilore Oludipe, Programmes Manager at Co-creation HUB (CcHUB); Mayenzeke Baza, Chief Investment and Development Officer at CEEIT; and Miebaka Anga, Strategic Partner Manager at YouTube.
Amadou Daffe, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Gebeya, urged young Africans to move beyond experimenting with AI and use it to create products and services that generate income.
“Knowledge is in the pocket. The question is, what do you do with it?” Daffe said.

He argued that the practical challenge is helping creators recognise and pursue the commercial possibilities of the technology. Drawing on Gebeya’s experience, he highlighted the importance of local-language capabilities and local-currency payment options in making digital tools more accessible to African users.

The panel was moderated by Omolabake Olagunju, Programme Manager at CcHUB Creative Economy. Joining Daffe were Malik Afegbua, Founder of Slick City Media; Uchechi Arinze, Creative Director and Founder of CHéCHI; Ibrahim Tsado Yisa, Africa Director at Udu Technologies; and Oo Nwoye, Founder of TechCircle.

The discussion examined how AI is changing the creation and consumption of creative work, including questions of ownership and originality. Contributions also explored intentional storytelling, cultural representation, algorithmic bias and the cost of accessing digital tools, highlighting the need to consider whose stories are being told and how African cultures are represented.

Emeka Onyia, Afreximbank’s Director, Digital Business and Innovation, described the session as an inaugural activity for the Afreximbank Innovation Lab. He said AI was lowering some of the equipment and production barriers facing creators, while stressing that skills and the effective use of tools remained essential. He also outlined the Lab’s ambition to bring people together to develop ideas and technologies that support African trade.

With a format centred on working projects rather than proposals alone, the Create-Thon combined practical technology access, mentorship and industry exposure. Gebeya also acknowledged IREX’s support for the initiative.

For Afreximbank, the competition forms part of its broader work through CANEX to develop and commercialise Africa’s creative and cultural industries, helping creators reach markets, attract partners and retain more value from their work.

African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) is a Pan-African multilateral financial institution mandated to finance and promote intra- and extra-African trade. For over 30 years, the Bank has been deploying innovative structures to deliver financing solutions that support the transformation of the structure of Africa’s trade, accelerating industrialisation and intra-regional trade, thereby boosting economic expansion in Africa.

A strong supporter of the African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA), Afreximbank has launched a Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) that was adopted by the African Union (AU) as the payment and settlement platform to underpin the implementation of the AfCFTA.

Working with the AfCFTA Secretariat and the AU, the Bank has set up a US$10 billion Adjustment Fund to support countries effectively participating in the AfCFTA. At the end of December 2025, Afreximbank’s total assets and contingencies stood at over US$48.5 billion, and its shareholder funds amounted to US$8.4 billion.

Afreximbank has investment grade ratings assigned by China Chengxin International Credit Rating Co., Ltd (CCXI) (AAA), GCR (A), Japan Credit Rating Agency (JCR) (A-), Moody’s (Baa2) and S&P Global Ratings (BBB+). The Bank is headquartered in Cairo, Egypt.

items.description: A Kwale KCSE supervisor was abducted and beaten after rejecting a KSh 50,000 cheating bribe. Police are investigating the attack at Vingurugani school in Kwale.

Kwale - A Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) supervisor is recovering at home after being abducted and severely beaten by suspected Form Four candidates in Kinango Sub-County, Kwale County , following his refusal to allow cheating during the ongoing Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examinations.
The supervisor had been assigned to oversee exams at Vingurugani Secondary School when he intercepted unauthorised materials that a teacher had smuggled into the examination room.

He confiscated the papers and secured them as evidence, but the materials were subsequently stolen from his locker.

He was then summoned to the Kinango education offices, where a quality assurance official allegedly pressured him to cooperate with the teachers involved. On Monday, he was offered KSh 50,000 to look the other way on the malpractice, an offer he firmly declined.

The assault took place on the evening of Wednesday, November 11. After warning him the previous day that they would attack him upon his return, the students carried out their threat. The supervisor suffered severe cuts to his head and a fractured hand during the ordeal.
He told NTV that he feigned death in order to survive, and his attackers left him for dead after stealing the little money he had on him.

The attackers also made clear their motive and their anger at him specifically.

The supervisor has since filed a report at Kinango Police Station. Detectives have launched investigations to identify all individuals involved in the attack and to establish the full extent of the alleged conspiracy, which the supervisor suspects involves multiple parties.
Despite reporting the matter to authorities, he says he continues to live in fear and believes the network behind the scheme extends beyond the students who carried out the assault.

Data Shows 78% of Kenya’s Building Collapse Deaths Happen on Sites
items.description: Building collapses in Nairobi killed ten in 24 hours. See Stats Kenya data, IEK demands and what Nairobi County says on approvals, audits and enforcement.
content: Nine to ten workers died on Nairobi construction sites between Friday and Saturday, and the data shows the deaths follow a pattern.

Stats Kenya, a data research company, has logged at least 84 building collapses in Kenya since January 2020 , which killed at least 102 people. Nairobi accounts for 31 of those collapses and 39 of the deaths.

The Institution of Engineers of Kenya (IEK) wants investigations and nationwide audits. Nairobi City County says its Development Control Policy 2026 and Integrated Development Plan already target the gaps. For developers, lenders and buyers off plan, the question is whether enforcement now matches the paperwork.

The Eastleigh collapse on 23 October 2026 killed eight, the highest toll in the Stats Kenya dataset. The Syokimau slab failure followed on 13 November, and the Riverside wall failed on 14 November. All three buildings were under construction.

IEK separates the last two: it points to temporary works and concrete placement at Syokimau, and to the excavation support system and retaining walls at Riverside. It says these are “not conclusions on cause or responsibility.”

At Syokimau, police said 405 workers were on site and all were accounted for. Duncan Ochieng, the assistant inspector general of police in charge of disaster management, said: “So far we have confirmed six bodies, but also five people have been rushed to Imara Daima Hospital.”
At Riverside, Nairobi County said 39 workers were on site when the wall gave way, and the Kenya Red Cross sent action teams and ambulances.
Stats Kenya’s figures show where the risk sits. Of 102 deaths, 80 occurred at buildings under construction or demolition. Occupied buildings account for far fewer.

Most victims are workers. Neighbours, passers by and traders also die when a structure falls onto homes, shops and roads. That puts the cost on payrolls, site contractors and insurers before it reaches tenants.
Murang’a recorded the most deaths per collapse. At least four Nairobi collapses fell in Kamukunji Sub County, which includes Eastleigh, Gikomba and Shauri Moyo.

Kenya recorded 5 to 14 collapses a year from 2020 to 2025, with 14 the peak in 2022. By mid November 2026 the count stood at 25 collapses and 38 deaths. Stats Kenya cautions that older reports are harder to find online, so earlier years likely read low. It also notes that 37 of the 84 collapses fell in March to May, the long rains, though most reports give no cause.

The National Construction Authority (NCA) registers contractors and projects. In a 2018 assessment of 14,895 buildings, it found 10,791 needed demolition or strengthening before safe use, and only 2,194 qualified as safe. Its 2020 report counted 87 collapses in the previous five years, with about 200 deaths. In 2022 it inspected 26,060 projects and suspended 18,192, or 69.8%, for failing building regulations.
The 2018 and 2020 figures are reported by The Star .

The county names collapse as a problem in its own policy. The Executive Summary of the Nairobi City County Development Control Policy (final version dated 14 July 2026) lists buildings built without approval, buildings that depart from approval conditions, and the “collapse of buildings due to weak and unstable structures.”
It says the county has deployed technical staff to sub counties, run periodic audits of the built environment and stepped up enforcement.
The plan sets numerical targets for statutory inspections. It budgets KSh 85 million across five years for surveillance and statutory inspections to monitor developments.

Governor Johnson Sakaja addressed Eastleigh directly on 24 October. He said county records show an application for a 15 storey building with a basement was submitted and never granted. In his words: “The application was never granted, meaning there is no approval for this construction.”

He said a change of user application for the plot was approved in 2024, the Urban Planning Committee raised concerns in November 2024, and an enforcement order followed earlier this year. The county sent its documents to the police and the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) and called for investigation of the architect, physical planner and engineering firm named in its records.

More than 200 files sit at the Director of Public Prosecutions’ office and asked for prosecution powers to return to the county, as KBC reported . Capital FM reported a counter claim: the DPP’s office said City Hall never submitted an inquiry file on the Eastleigh collapse.

IEK addressed national and county governments, the NCA, the Engineers Board of Kenya (EBK), the Directorate of Occupational Safety and Health Services and the National Building Inspectorate. It asked for independent technical investigations, preservation of evidence and a halt to work in affected areas until safety clearance. I

t also asked for registered engineers on design and supervision until the Occupation Certificate issues, risk based audits of high risk projects, and a national review of safety regulations “with clear timelines and public reporting.”

The county’s tools and IEK’s demands overlap on three points: engineer supervision, inspection and enforcement. They differ on who investigates. IEK wants independence and EBK discipline for engineers found culpable. The county has referred matters to police and the DCI.
A project with an approval gap faces stop orders and demolition risk under the county’s planned enforcement rules. Lenders carry that risk on construction loans.

Off plan buyers carry it through delays. Sites that pass inspection keep the permit and Occupation Certificate path open, and the county has tied that certificate to full payment of the Development Impact Fee.

items.title: Kenya marks World Diabetes Day with Free screenings in Nairobi
items.description: Kenya marked World Diabetes Day with a three-day free health screening programme for diabetes and thyroid-related conditions. The programme concluded on the sidelines of the 10th Annual Lions Diabetes Symposium, highlighting the importance of early detection and regular health checks in addressing non-communicable diseases.- Advertisement - The screening initiative was conducted through Merck’s ThyroAfrica programme […]
content: Kenya marked World Diabetes Day with a three-day free health screening programme for diabetes and thyroid-related conditions.
The programme concluded on the sidelines of the 10th Annual Lions Diabetes Symposium, highlighting the importance of early detection and regular health checks in addressing non-communicable diseases.

The screening initiative was conducted through Merck’s ThyroAfrica programme and included Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) tests to help identify potential thyroid disorders, as well as Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) tests to assess blood sugar levels for supporting diabetes detection and management.

Speaking during the screening activation at Lion’s Hospital, Dr. Rilwan Adan, Physician and Diabetologist, and Head of the Lions Diabetes Care Centre in Nairobi, emphasised the importance of screening for both diabetes and thyroid disorders, noting that the two conditions can coexist and should not be considered in isolation.

“When screening for one condition, it is important to screen for the other as well, because thyroid disorders and diabetes can occur together. Taking an integrated approach to screening helps promote early detection and more comprehensive care”, said Dr. Rilwan.

She further highlighted the importance of community-based screening, noting that despite the increasing incidence of diabetes and thyroid disorders, many cases remain undiagnosed for extended periods, partly due to limited routine health checks and low health-seeking behaviour.

“As the number of cases continues to rise, many people are still living with these conditions without knowing it. Community screening is, therefore important, because it takes health services directly to the people rather than waiting for them to come to health facilities. This helps create opportunities for early detection and timely intervention”, she said.
Across African countries, thyroid disorders remain largely invisible within national health priorities and broader non-communicable disease (NCD) strategies.
A lack of reliable data, limited screening and labs coverage & pricing schemes, as well as low awareness among both patients and healthcare providers, contribute to late diagnosis and poor outcomes.
So, Thyroid Disease is often identified at an advanced stage, which increases mortality, treatment costs, and the overall economic burden on families and health systems.

Speaking on the broader significance of the initiative, Merck General Manager for Sub-Saharan Africa, John Ndeti, noted that World Diabetes Day represents a culmination of year-long efforts to raise awareness, expand access to screening and strengthen healthcare workers’ capacity to address noncommunicable diseases.
“This is not an effort that happens on World Diabetes Day alone. We have been carrying out awareness, screening and healthcare worker empowerment activities throughout the year.

“Early detection can save lives and improve quality of life. We, therefore, encourage people to be proactive about their health, by going for regular screening, rather than waiting until symptoms appear before seeking medical attention”, said Ndeti.
To close these gaps, in April 2025, Merck launched ThyroAfrica in collaboration with hospitals, laboratories, researchers and policymakers
As part of this initiative, members of the public can also use a free 2-minute ThyroidAware Symptom Checker, to determine their Risk level, then seek appropriate medical attention.

items.title: George Ruto: Video Shows 1st Son's 98 SACCO Matatu Performing Stunts Before Accident
items.description: Footage appears to show George Ruto's Baba Yaga and rival matatu Detroit racing before a Nairobi-Kiserian crash on November 13, raising questions about road safety.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
George Ruto's prized matatu , Baba Yaga, is out of service after a collision that left it and a rival vehicle badly damaged.
Newly obtained footage, however, is raising uncomfortable questions about the events leading up to the crash.
The accident took place on the night of Friday, November 13, along Route 125, the Nairobi-Kiserian corridor that Baba Yaga operates under Ruto's 98 SACCO PSV line.
The John Wick-themed matatu, one of the more eye-catching vehicles in the fleet, reportedly ploughed into the rear of another well-known matatu on the route, Detroit.
George Ruto’s Baba Yaga matatu involved in yet another accident

A source familiar with the incident told TUKO.co.ke that the two vehicles had been competing on the road when the collision took place.
Images and footage captured at the scene told a stark story. Baba Yaga's front end bore the full force of the impact, with its bumper, grille and body panels caved in.

Debris and dislodged interior fittings lay scattered around the vehicle. Detroit did not escape unscathed either, with its rear section sustaining significant damage. No fatalities or official injury figures were reported in the initial coverage of the incident.
The crew running Baba Yaga under the Raptors banner addressed the situation on the matatu's official Instagram account the following morning, Saturday, November 14.

TUKO.co.ke has obtained video footage that purportedly captures events in the moments leading up to the collision.
In the clip, two Route 125 matatus appear to engage in a rat race, the kind of competitive speed duel that has long been a fixture of Nairobi's nganya culture.
The vehicles are seen driving in the wrong lane of a two-way road, overtaking other motorists at considerable speed.
What stands out beyond the driving itself is the behaviour on board. Some occupants are visible hanging out of the doors and windows, while others can be seen swaying as the matatus accelerate.
The footage does not capture the moment of impact itself, and while it appears to show risky behaviour shortly before the crash, it does not independently confirm the precise cause of the collision.
The video does, however, put a spotlight on the culture of rat racing on Route 125, and the safety risks it creates not just for passengers but for other road users as well.

Baba Yaga is among the more distinctive matatus associated with George and has built a following among fans of Nairobi's vibrant PSV scene.
Its crew's vow to return suggests repairs are already being planned, but the footage circulating online may yet attract attention from road safety authorities.
TUKO.co.ke also highlighted facts about George’s 98 SACCO and the fares its matatus charge on Route 125.
The Sacco’s customised fleet has attracted Gen Z commuters, while its rapid expansion has prompted debate over competition and oversight in Nairobi’s public transport sector.

content: Belgium will take on Italy in a must win UEFA Nations League encounter on Sunday evening, if they are to stand a chance at qualification.
The red devils come into the game in third place in Group A1 with nine points, one less than their opponents Italy and France.
The fixture is particularly intriguing because the two nations have already met once in this campaign, with Belgium winning 2-0 in Rome in September.
However, Italy have responded impressively since that defeat and arrive in Brussels sitting at the top of the group after an outstanding 3-1 victory over France on Thursday.
Belgium, meanwhile, kept their qualification hopes alive with a 2-1 comeback win over Türkiye.

With only the top two teams progressing to the quarterfinals, this is effectively a qualification decider for Belgium, while Italy have the luxury of knowing that a draw is enough to take them through.

items.title: AFC Leopards target victory against Mombasa United in Kenya Premier league
items.description: AFC Leopards will today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, take on Mombasa United in a Kenyan Premier League encounter as Ingwe seeks to maintain its unbeaten run and strengthen its position in the 2026/27 season.
content: AFC Leopards will today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, take on Mombasa United in a Kenyan Premier League encounter as Ingwe seeks to maintain its unbeaten run and strengthen its position in the 2026/27 season.
The match is scheduled to kick off at 3:30 PM EAT at Wang’uru Stadium, with both sides targeting crucial points for different reasons.

AFC Leopards head into the encounter unbeaten in their opening six league matches, having recorded two victories and four draws. Their 2-0 victory over Kakamega Homeboyz on November 1 was an important result before they settled for a goalless draw against 3K FC on November 7. Ingwe currently has 10 points and occupies third position in the league standings.

Head coach Fred Ambani has emphasised the need for his players to improve their finishing, pointing out that missed scoring opportunities have cost the team valuable points in previous matches. Ambani wants his attacking players to remain composed in front of goal and make better use of the chances created.

On the other hand, Mombasa United head into the fixture under pressure after collecting just one point from their opening six matches. The newly promoted side sits bottom of the 18-team standings, having suffered five defeats and recorded one draw.

In their most recent league outing on November 7, Mombasa United suffered a 3-2 defeat against Shabana at Mbaraki Sports Club. This followed earlier losses against Migori Youth, who beat them 2-0, and KCB, who secured a 3-1 victory.

Assistant coach Mohamed Ahmed Mchulla has revealed that the team has been working on its defensive weaknesses, particularly dealing with set-pieces and maintaining defensive organisation after losing possession. He has also stressed the importance of improving their finishing if they are to start collecting positive results.
Captain Hakimu Msami has also expressed confidence that the players have learned from their previous mistakes and are ready to fight for their first league victory of the campaign.

Meanwhile, AFC Leopards have some injury concerns, with Eric Balecho and Samwel Semo reportedly sidelined, while the fitness of Kayci Odhiambo and Vincent Mahiga remains under assessment. Goalkeeper Tom Ikara will be one of the key players for Ingwe, having kept five clean sheets in the club’s opening six league matches.

The encounter presents an important opportunity for both sides. AFC Leopards will be looking to extend their unbeaten run and remain in contention for the league title, while Mombasa United will be desperate to secure their first victory of the season and move away from the bottom of the table.

A past interview featuring Ohangla star Onyango Jasuba, popularly known as Nyakwar Dayo or Mandela, has begun circulating widely online following news of his passing.
Jasuba died on Saturday, November 14, after a short illness, leaving the Ohangla music community in deep mourning.
The resurfaced clip has since drawn significant attention, with many fans revisiting the musician's own words about life in the entertainment industry.
In the interview, the exact date of which remains unclear, Jasuba addressed a song he recorded titled Mwanduni Emanegi, loosely translated as "your wealth is what is killing you."

The conversation then moved to the lifestyle typically associated with performers, with the interviewer raising the question of whether alcohol and promiscuity contributed to the struggles of musicians.

items.title: Kenya contains imported Ebola case as country moves towards disease-free status
items.description: Kenya contains imported Ebola case as country moves towards disease-free status Kenya Association of Travel Agents
content: Kenya has contained an imported Ebola outbreak without community transmission, with authorities confirming that all patients have recovered or been discharged and the country now entering a 42-day countdown towards an official declaration that it is free of the disease.

The outbreak originated from a Kenyan national who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and travelled through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on October 3, 2026. The Ministry of Health confirmed the country’s first case of Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease on October 6.
The case triggered an extensive public health response involving isolation, laboratory testing, contact tracing and monitoring to prevent further transmission.

Kenya subsequently recorded eight secondary infections, bringing the total to nine confirmed cases. All eight were linked to the initial imported case, involving four family members and four healthcare workers. Crucially, all secondary cases were identified among people already under quarantine, and health authorities reported no transmission into the wider community.
The outbreak resulted in two deaths, while seven patients recovered.

The Ministry of Health identified and monitored 135 contacts linked to the initial case, including individuals in Kenya and abroad. The final patient was discharged on November 11, while the remaining 11 contacts completed their monitoring period without developing symptoms.

The 42-day countdown began on November 12 and, if no new infections are detected, Kenya is expected to be declared Ebola-free on December 23, 2026. The period represents twice the virus’s maximum 21-day incubation period, in line with World Health Organization protocols.

The successful containment effort highlights Kenya’s public health surveillance and emergency response capabilities, including early case detection, laboratory confirmation, isolation facilities, contact tracing and coordination between national and county health authorities.

The World Health Organization has also reported no evidence of transmission outside the identified cluster and no new confirmed cases in Kenya since October 19. In its latest disease outbreak update, the organisation advised against imposing travel or trade restrictions on countries responding to the regional health event.

For Kenya’s travel and tourism industry, the distinction between an imported case and sustained local transmission is particularly important. The outbreak did not result in widespread community transmission or a nationwide shutdown of economic and social activities.

The government has maintained that Kenya remains open for international travel, tourism, trade and business, with no domestic restrictions on movement or public gatherings. Enhanced health screening and surveillance at points of entry remain in place as precautionary measures.

While the outbreak in the DRC continues to require regional vigilance, Kenya’s experience demonstrates the importance of effective disease surveillance and rapid containment in protecting public health and maintaining international travel connectivity.

items.title: Kenyans urged to embrace regular diabetes and thyroid screening
items.description: Kenyans have been urged to embrace regular health screening and early medical check-ups as part of efforts to curb the rising burden of non-communicable diseases, including diabetes and thyroid disorders.
content: Kenyans have been urged to embrace regular health screening and early medical check-ups as part of efforts to curb the rising burden of non-communicable diseases, including diabetes and thyroid disorders.
The call was made as Kenya marked World Diabetes Day through a three-day free health screening programme at Lions SightFirst Eye Hospital in Loresho, Nairobi.

The initiative, which concluded on Saturday, November 14, was held alongside the 10th Annual Lions Diabetes Symposium and offered members of the public free tests for diabetes and thyroid-related conditions.

The screening was conducted under Merck’s ThyroAfrica programme, featuring Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) tests to detect possible thyroid disorders and HbA1c tests to assess average blood sugar levels and support diabetes diagnosis and management.
The pilot programme, which brought together diabetes and thyroid screening, targeted approximately 500 people in Nairobi.

Speaking during the exercise, Dr. Rilwan Adan, a Physician and Diabetologist and Head of the Lions Diabetes Care Centre, emphasised the need for integrated screening, noting that diabetes and thyroid disorders can occur simultaneously and should not be treated in isolation.

Dr. Adan further warned that despite the increasing cases of diabetes and thyroid disorders, many people continue to live with the conditions unknowingly due to limited routine medical check-ups and low health-seeking behaviour.
She urged Kenyans to prioritise regular health examinations, saying early detection remains critical in preventing complications and improving treatment.

Merck General Manager for Sub-Saharan Africa John Ndeti urged Kenyans to embrace regular medical screening, saying early detection remains critical in managing non-communicable diseases. ‎ ‎Ndeti revealed that an earlier screening exercise at Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Mwea reached 147 people, including 46 screened for thyroid disorders and 101 for diabetes. ‎ ‎The Nairobi initiative, which targeted approximately 500 people, coincided with the 10th Annual Lions Diabetes Symposium and forms part of Merck’s broader ThyroAfrica programme launched in April 2025 to improve awareness, strengthen diagnostic capacity and expand access to thyroid care across Africa. ‎ ‎The programme also encourages members of the public to use a free two-minute ThyroidAware symptom checker to assess their risk and seek medical attention where necessary. ‎

content: Kenya marked World Diabetes Day with a three-day free health screening programme for diabetes and thyroid-related conditions.
The programme concluded on the sidelines of the 10th Annual Lions Diabetes Symposium, highlighting the importance of early detection and regular health checks in addressing non-communicable diseases.

The screening initiative was conducted through Merck’s ThyroAfrica programme and included Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) tests to help identify potential thyroid disorders, as well as Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) tests to assess blood sugar levels for supporting diabetes detection and management.

Speaking during the screening activation at Lion’s Hospital, Dr. Rilwan Adan, Physician and Diabetologist, and Head of the Lions Diabetes Care Centre in Nairobi, emphasised the importance of screening for both diabetes and thyroid disorders, noting that the two conditions can coexist and should not be considered in isolation.

“When screening for one condition, it is important to screen for the other as well, because thyroid disorders and diabetes can occur together. Taking an integrated approach to screening helps promote early detection and more comprehensive care”, said Dr. Rilwan.

She further highlighted the importance of community-based screening, noting that despite the increasing incidence of diabetes and thyroid disorders, many cases remain undiagnosed for extended periods, partly due to limited routine health checks and low health-seeking behaviour.

“As the number of cases continues to rise, many people are still living with these conditions without knowing it. Community screening is, therefore important, because it takes health services directly to the people rather than waiting for them to come to health facilities. This helps create opportunities for early detection and timely intervention”, she said.
Across African countries, thyroid disorders remain largely invisible within national health priorities and broader non-communicable disease (NCD) strategies.
A lack of reliable data, limited screening and labs coverage & pricing schemes, as well as low awareness among both patients and healthcare providers, contribute to late diagnosis and poor outcomes.
So, Thyroid Disease is often identified at an advanced stage, which increases mortality, treatment costs, and the overall economic burden on families and health systems.

Speaking on the broader significance of the initiative, Merck General Manager for Sub-Saharan Africa, John Ndeti, noted that World Diabetes Day represents a culmination of year-long efforts to raise awareness, expand access to screening and strengthen healthcare workers’ capacity to address noncommunicable diseases.
“This is not an effort that happens on World Diabetes Day alone. We have been carrying out awareness, screening and healthcare worker empowerment activities throughout the year.

“Early detection can save lives and improve quality of life. We, therefore, encourage people to be proactive about their health, by going for regular screening, rather than waiting until symptoms appear before seeking medical attention”, said Ndeti.
To close these gaps, in April 2025, Merck launched ThyroAfrica in collaboration with hospitals, laboratories, researchers and policymakers
As part of this initiative, members of the public can also use a free 2-minute ThyroidAware Symptom Checker, to determine their Risk level, then seek appropriate medical attention.
